title: Assembly Quiz
description: Review the 12 starter lessons. The questions name the example to revisit. Take your time, use the lessons, and read the reason after each answer.

questions.code:
global _start
section .text
_start:
    mov rdi, 5
    mov rax, 60
    syscall
questions.question: rdi is a register: a tiny storage place in the processor. Linux exit reads its status from rdi. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: mov puts 5 in rdi. The exit syscall takes its code from that register. Exit codes are only 0 to 255; use small values in these lessons.

questions.code:
global _start
section .text
_start:
    mov rbx, 3
    mov rdi, rbx
    mov rax, 60
    syscall
questions.question: mov copies a value. It does not erase the source register. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: rbx first receives 3. Copying it into rdi passes 3 to exit. The destination comes first in NASM syntax.

questions.code:
global _start
section .text
_start:
    mov rdi, 3
    add rdi, 2
    mov rax, 60
    syscall
questions.question: add changes its first register by adding the second value. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: add changes rdi from 3 to 5 before exit reads it. The add instruction changes the destination register.

questions.code:
global _start
section .text
_start:
    mov rdi, 8
    sub rdi, 3
    mov rax, 60
    syscall
questions.question: sub subtracts the second value from the first register. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: sub changes rdi from 8 to 5. Keep the result within a small positive range for exit codes.

questions.code:
global _start
section .text
_start:
    mov rdi, 3
    imul rdi, rdi, 2
    mov rax, 60
    syscall
questions.question: imul multiplies signed integers. This form stores the result in its first register. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: imul multiplies the value 3 by 2 and stores 6 in rdi. Large results can overflow a register.

questions.code:
global _start
section .text
_start:
    mov rax, 8
    xor rdx, rdx
    mov rbx, 3
    div rbx
    mov rdi, rax
    mov rax, 60
    syscall
questions.question: div divides rdx:rax by its input. For this small positive example, clear rdx first. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: rdx is cleared so the dividend is 8. Division by 3 leaves quotient 2 in rax. Never divide by zero. The remainder is in rdx, not rax.

questions.code:
global _start
section .text
_start:
    mov rdi, 5
    and rdi, 1
    mov rax, 60
    syscall
questions.question: and keeps only bits that are 1 in both inputs. A final bit of 1 marks an odd number. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The binary form of 5 ends with 1. AND with 1 keeps only that bit. Bitwise and is an operation on bits, not a high-level if statement.

questions.code:
global _start
section .text
_start:
    mov rdi, 0
    mov rbx, 5
    cmp rbx, 5
    je .same
    jmp .done
.same:
    mov rdi, 1
.done:
    mov rax, 60
    syscall
questions.question: cmp compares values and sets flags. je jumps when the compared values are equal. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: cmp finds equality, so je reaches .same and sets rdi to 1. A jump uses flags from the previous comparison; avoid changing them first.

questions.code:
global _start
section .text
_start:
    mov rcx, 3
    mov rdi, 0
.again:
    add rdi, 2
    dec rcx
    jnz .again
    mov rax, 60
    syscall
questions.question: A label names a place in the code. jnz repeats while the last result was not zero. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The loop adds 2 three times. The decreasing counter eventually reaches zero. A loop needs a counter or rule that eventually stops.

questions.code:
global _start
section .text
_start:
    push 7
    pop rdi
    mov rax, 60
    syscall
questions.question: push places a value on the stack. pop takes the most recent value back. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: push stores 7 on the stack. pop places that most recent value in rdi. Keep pushes and pops balanced.

questions.code:
global _start
section .text
_start:
    mov rdi, 4
    call twice
    mov rax, 60
    syscall
twice:
    add rdi, rdi
    ret
questions.question: call saves a return address and jumps. ret returns to the instruction after call. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: call enters twice with 4. The routine doubles rdi and ret returns with 8. A routine reached by call should return with ret, not fall into unrelated code.

questions.code:
global _start
section .data
message: db "Hi", 10
section .text
_start:
    mov rax, 1
    mov rdi, 1
    lea rsi, [rel message]
    mov rdx, 3
    syscall
    mov rdi, 0
    mov rax, 60
    syscall
questions.question: The write system call uses rax=1, rdi=1 for standard output, an address in rsi and a length in rdx. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
questions.explanation: The data contains two letters and one newline byte. Linux writes three bytes, then exits with zero. The length counts bytes, including the newline byte.
